'''Ruth Landshoff Vollmer''' (1903–1982 [[New York City]]), was a German-born [[conceptual art]]ist who lived and worked in the United States.

== Early life ==
Born in [[Munich]] in 1903 as Ruth Landshoff. Her father, [[Ludwig Landshoff]], was a musicologist and conductor<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Einstein |first=Alfred |date=1942 |title=In Memoriam: Ludwig Landshoff (b. June 3, 1874 – d. September 20, 1941) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/739218 |journal=The Musical Quarterly |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=241–247 |issn=0027-4631 |jstor=739218}}</ref> and her mother, Philippine Wiesengrund Landshoff, was an soprano opera singer. Her brother, [[Hermann Landshoff]], became a photographer.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Kronthaler |first=Helmut |title=Allgemeines Künstler-Lexikon: Die bildenden Künstler aller Zeiten und Völker |publisher=De Gruyter |year=2022 |isbn=9783110550658 |editor-last=Beyer |editor-first=Andreas |volume=114 |pages=56–57 |chapter=Vollmer, Ruth, (geb. Landshoff) |editor-last2=Savoy |editor-first2=Bénédicte |editor-last3=Tegethoff |editor-first3=Wolf}}</ref> Their family was Jewish, and their circle of friends in the 1920s included [[Gerhart Hauptmann|Gerhardt Hauptmann]], [[Thomas Mann]], [[Albert Einstein]], and [[Paul Klee]], among other writers, scientists, musicians and artists.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Lovatt |first=Anna |title=On Ruth Vollmer and Minimalism's Marginalia |journal=Art History: Journal of the Association of Art Historians |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=151–169 |issn=0141-6790}}</ref> At age 19 she moved from Bavaria to Berlin to work as an [[au pair]].<ref name=":0" /> Ruth began to learn to draw in 1922.<ref name=":1" /> She maintained an interest in the visual arts,<ref name=":0" /> and took the advice of her father to draw every day.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}} She also had many connections to the teachers and students at the [[Bauhaus]], such as Erich Mendelssohn, who had designed their Berlin apartment.<ref name=":0" /> In 1930 she married the pediatrician Hermann Vollmer, whom she had met in Berlin. Ruth and Hermann moved from Germany (via Liverpool)<ref name=":1" /> to New York in 1935.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Ruth began work designing window displays for [[Bonwit Teller]], [[Tiffany & Co.|Tiffany's]], [[Lord & Taylor]], and other department stores. Her displays experimented with wire, steel, and copper mesh to create figural forms. In 1943, Vollmer became a U.S. citizen. In 1944 she received a commission from the [[Museum of Modern Art]] for its fifteenth anniversary exhibition, "Art in Progress." Vollmer continued to work with wire mesh and exhibited her work ''Composition in Space'' at the Museum of Modern Art in their 1948 exhibition "Elements of Stage Design." In 1950, she was commissioned to create a mural for the lobby of 575 Madison, where she created a large wall relief that used wire rods and wire mesh to play with light, texture, and transparency. Vollmer visited [[Alberto Giacometti|Giacometti]] for a second time during the summer of 1951. During the 1950s she begins to works with clay as well. Additionally, in 1954 she began to teach at the Children's Art Center at the [[Ethical Culture Fieldston School|Fieldston School]] in [[Riverdale, Bronx|Riverdale]] and continued to teach until the mid-sixties. In 1960, she participated in the [[New York University]] discussion series "Artists on Art" with her friend [[Robert Motherwell]]. The year 1960 proved to be a significant one for Ruth Vollmer: she had her first solo exhibition at [[Betty Parsons|Betty Parson]]'s Section Eleven gallery space. Throughout the 1960s Vollmer continued to work with bronze and to show her work at the Betty Parsons Gallery. In 1963, she joined the [[American Abstract Artists]] (AAA) and showed her in their exhibitions from 1963 on. By 1970 Vollmer's practice had taken on a new dimension, exploring complex geometrical forms and mathematical concepts, particularly [[Spiral|spirals]] and [[Platonic solid|platonic solids]]. [[Sol LeWitt]] wrote a short essay on Vollmer's work for ''Studio International'' titled "Ruth Vollmer: Mathematical Forms." In 1971 Ruth Vollmer participated in the protest of the cancellation of the [[Hans Haacke]] at [[Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum|The Solomon R. Guggenheim]] exhibition by writing a letter to the museum's director, [[Thomas M. Messer|Thomas Messer]]. In 1976, she had a large one-person exhibition at the [[Neuberger Museum of Art]].

Vollmer hosted artists such as [[Robert Smithson]], [[Donald Judd]], [[Sol LeWitt]], [[Carl Andre]], and [[Eva Hesse]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rubenstein |first=Charlotte Streifer |title=American Women Sculptors: A History of Women Working in Three Dimensions |publisher=G.K. Hall |year=1990 |isbn=0816187320 |location=Boston |pages=391–392 |language=en-US}}</ref> at "[[Salon (gathering)|salons]]" in her apartment on [[Eighth Avenue (Manhattan)|Central Park West]].<ref name=":0" />

By 2022, Vollmer's work would be found in the following public collections: [[Kunstmuseum Winterthur]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Unsere Sammlung |url=https://kmw.zetcom.net/de/collection/?f=relatedWorks_560_Ruth+Vollmer |access-date=2024-02-09 |website=Kunst Museum Winterthur Katalog Online}}</ref> the Museum of Modern Art, the [[National Gallery of Art]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Collection Search Results: Vollmer, Ruth |url=https://www.nga.gov/collection-search-result.html?artist=Vollmer,%20Ruth |access-date=2024-02-09 |website=National Gallery of Art}}</ref> the Whitney Museum of American Art,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Art & Artists: Ruth Vollmer |url=https://whitney.org/artists/1374 |access-date=2024-02-09 |website=Whitney Museum of American Art |language=en-US}}</ref> the Neuberger Museum of Art, the [[Worcester Art Museum]], and the [[Rose Art Museum]] at [[Brandeis University]].

In 1982, Ruth Vollmer died after a long battle with [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer]]'s. A majority of her personal art collection of over one hundred sculptures, paintings, and drawings was donated to MoMA. Her personal art collection included works by [[Carl Andre]], [[Mel Bochner]], Eva Hesse, Sol LeWitt, [[Ad Reinhardt]], [[Frank Stella]], [[Agnes Martin]], and [[Chryssa]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://brandeis.on.worldcat.org/oclc/81963895?databaseList=638|title=Ruth Vollmer 1961–1978 : thinking the line|last=Vollmer|first=Ruth|date=2006|publisher=Hatje Cantz|isbn=9783775717861|location=Ostfildern}}</ref>
